data.name: Boom Island
data.detailed_description:
Imagine being stranded on an island in the early 1900's, being a only survivor in a experimental plane crash. However, the island you crashed on is not a normal island, its Boom Island! Engage yourself in this arcade style first person shooter, where the main objective is to shoot highly explosive bouncing beach balls while staying alive. Immerse yourself with vintage effects and arcade style gameplay.

Gamemodes:


  • Survival:
    A classic style of play where your objective is to survive an infinite amount of beach balls in various waves, as you survive the waves, your difficulty will gradually increase until you get blown up.

  • Economy
    In economy mode, you will survive the balls while collecting money by killing them. You can use that money to buy various weapons, ammo, and health in the in-game shop.

  • Protection:
    Similar aspect to survival, however your arsenal and mobility has greatly changed. Get strapped in to a giant mounted machine gun on your destroyed plane, as you flawlessly penetrate the explosive beach balls with ammunition, not being a problem.

    More features:



  • Partial Controller Support.
    Boom island allows you to use a controller to play. However you need to navigate through the menus with a mouse, as well as manually configure the controller binding in the control settings.

  • Graphics Customization
    You can adjust a ton of video settings such as v-sync, textures, Anti Aliasing and many more.


  • Custom Controls
    Change keys and their mappings to your own liking in the settings.



    What are you waiting for? Go head to the island and good luck.

reviews.review:
Boom Island takes the familiar wave-survival shooter formula and gives it an intentionally ridiculous identity. Instead of fighting soldiers, zombies, or alien creatures, players find themselves stranded after an experimental plane crash in the early 1900s and must defend themselves against bouncing beach balls capable of exploding on contact. Developed by Caden Goodwin and published by csgood, it is a compact indie first-person shooter that prioritizes arcade action and absurd humor over realism, elaborate storytelling, or complicated mechanics.

The premise is established quickly and largely exists to justify the action. After surviving the crash, the player discovers that the island is populated by increasingly dangerous explosive balls. Their bouncing movement makes them less predictable than ordinary stationary targets, forcing players to pay attention to distance, positioning, and aim. There is an amusing contrast between the vintage setting and the completely nonsensical enemies, giving the game a personality that distinguishes it from more conventional wave shooters. It is not particularly deep, but its willingness to embrace such a strange concept is part of its charm.

Survival mode offers the most straightforward version of the gameplay. Waves continue indefinitely and become progressively more difficult, leaving the player to survive for as long as possible. The lack of a conventional ending makes personal endurance the primary objective. It works well for quick sessions because there is little preparation required before the action begins. However, repetition inevitably becomes noticeable because the fundamental objective remains unchanged throughout the experience. Players who enjoy improving their performance and surviving increasingly intense waves will get more from this mode than those seeking structured missions or narrative progression.

Economy mode gives the shooting loop more substance by introducing money and resource management. Destroying enemies earns currency that can be spent on weapons, ammunition, and health. This creates a more satisfying sense of progression because every successful encounter contributes toward improving the player's chances during later waves. Deciding whether to purchase additional firepower, replenish ammunition, or restore health introduces simple strategic choices. It remains an arcade experience at heart, but the economy system provides an extra incentive to perform well and makes this mode feel more developed than pure endless survival.

Protection mode changes the pace by placing the player behind a large machine gun mounted to the wreckage of the aircraft. Mobility is sacrificed in exchange for substantial firepower, turning the experience into a stationary defensive challenge. Rather than constantly repositioning and carefully managing ordinary weapons, the focus becomes identifying incoming threats and maintaining sustained fire. It is mechanically simple, yet it provides enough contrast to keep the three modes from feeling completely interchangeable.

The game includes several customization features that are useful for a small independent release. Players can adjust graphical settings such as textures, anti-aliasing, and V-sync, while keyboard controls can be remapped according to personal preference. Partial controller support is available, although it is not completely seamless. Menu navigation still requires mouse input, and controller bindings may need to be manually configured. There is also a level editor, adding some creative potential beyond the standard modes and allowing players to experiment with the game's basic systems.

Visually, Boom Island is functional rather than technically impressive. Its vintage presentation complements the historical setting, but the environments, models, and effects remain relatively modest. That simplicity fits the game's lightweight nature and helps keep hardware requirements accessible. The sound and visual presentation mainly exist to support the immediate arcade gameplay instead of creating an especially immersive world. Anyone approaching it expecting the production quality of a major FPS should adjust expectations accordingly.

Steam Deck compatibility is currently best considered Unknown or Unverified rather than officially confirmed as Deck Verified or Playable. The game's modest hardware demands suggest that performance itself should not be its largest obstacle, but partial controller implementation is more significant. Since mouse interaction is required for menus and controller bindings need additional configuration, Steam Deck users may have to create or modify a Steam Input layout and use trackpad or touchscreen input for certain interactions. It should therefore not be treated as a completely seamless handheld experience without further testing.

The main weakness is ultimately limited depth. There are different modes, purchasing mechanics, adjustable settings, and a level editor, but everything revolves around shooting variations of the same explosive threat. Players looking for sophisticated enemy AI, extensive weapon progression, elaborate maps, boss encounters, or a lengthy campaign will find the package fairly thin. Conversely, its simplicity makes it easy to understand and suitable for short bursts when a player wants something uncomplicated and unusual.

Boom Island is ultimately an eccentric arcade FPS whose greatest strength is its willingness to commit to an absurd concept. Survival provides endless escalating action, Economy introduces a useful progression loop, and Protection offers a more stationary form of destruction. These elements cannot completely overcome the repetitive nature of the central mechanic, but they give the experience enough variation to make it more than a single-joke experiment. For players interested in obscure indie shooters and uncomplicated wave-based action, it offers a peculiar diversion that knows exactly what kind of game it wants to be.

Rating: 5/10
